text.p: The following are the main stories from Tuesday morning's Austrian newspapers:

- The civil servants union has cancelled all talks with representatives of the government and now demand talks with Chancellor Viktor Klima about the government's plans for spending cuts in the public sector. A general strike of Austria's civil servants was not decided upon.

- Economics Minister Hannes Farnleitner believes the government will cancel plans to introduce a road-pricing system for cars on Austria's motorways. Road pricing for trucks are expected only to be introduced on the major motorways.
- The European Union might demand Austria abolish its planned import limitations on cigarettes, experts say.
- Federal grid company Verbund chief Johannes Sereinig says European over-supply of electricity will push down prices even further.
- Social Affairs Minister Lore Hostasch plans to reduce pensions for high-income earners so that the budget will save up to 16 billion schillings over the next two years.
- Vienna's city government has declined allowing its holding-company AVZ, the majority shareholder of Bank Austria, to be checked by the town's audit office.
- Economics Minister Farnleitner plans to use eight billion schillings from the sale of Creditanstalt to Bank Austria to subsidise loss-making road-financing company Asfinag.

- Former German foreign minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher said at a meeting in Vienna that the European Union needs the single currency euro and eastward expansion. He does not expect EMU to be delayed.
- Fireproof materials producer Rath will pay a dividend of four schillings for 1996 as the company swung into the black.
- Italy's milk producer Parmalat says it is not interested in participating in milk producer Noem as it does not see any sense in such a move at the moment.
- Vienna's electricity company Wiener Stadtwerke will receive an additional five billion schillings from the city government in order to prepare for the liberalisation of the market.
- Big comanies are putting pressure on grid company Verbund as competition starts to creep into Austria's electricity market.
- Farnleitner plans to introduce a ban on selling goods under the introductory price.
- Savings banks union head Alfred Pachernigg calls the Vienna city council's plans with Bank Austria a massive attack against all savings banks.
